editorial_contributions.text:
This article is in two parts, both of which concern the Chow groups of cubic hypersurfaces over local fields. In the first part, the base field is a \(p\)-adic field, or indeed any \(C_2\) field, and the dimension of the hypersurface is large: the main result is the vanishing of the Chow group of classes of zero-cycles of degree zero when the dimension is at least \(10\). In the second part, an explicit example is constructed of a cubic threefold over the field \({\mathbb C}((v,t))\) with non-trivial Chow group of zero-cycles of degree zero. The author comments that, although this particular construction does not give such an example over \({\mathbb Q}_p\), the existence of such an example seems plausible.


Section~1 is devoted to proving the following result (Proposition 1.1): Let \(X\) be a cubic hypersurface of dimension at least \(10\) over a \(p\)-adic field \(K\). Then any two points of \(X(K)\) are \(R\)-equivalent: \(X(K)/R = \{*\}\).

Given that \(R\)-equivalence of two points implies rational equivalence of the corresponding zero-cycles, this implies that the Chow group \(\text{CH}_0^0(X)\) of zero-cycles of degree zero is also trivial.

The only facts used in proving Proposition~1.1 are the following: any quadratic form over \(K\) in at least five variables has a non-trivial zero; and any cubic form over \(K\) in at least ten variables has a non-trivial zero. The result is therefore also valid over any other field satisfying these requirements, and in particular over any \(C_2\) field.


The longer Section~2 is concerned with the cubic hypersurface 
\[
 X^3 + Y^3 + v Z^3 + t U^3 + tv V^3 = 0 
\]
 over the field \({\mathbb C}((v,t))\), or \({\mathbb C}((v))((t))\). The aim is to prove Proposition~2.1, stating that the Chow group \(\text{CH}_0^0\) of this threefold is non-trivial. The way this is achieved is through the explicit construction and study of a regular model over \({\mathbb C}((v))[t]\). This model is found by glueing together toric resolutions of the singularities of the given model. A study of the Chow groups of the various components of the special fibre of this model leads to the result.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: For \(d=2,3,4\) there exist a field \(F\) of cohomological dimension 1 and a del Pezzo surface over \(F\), of degree \(d\), which does not support a zero-cycle of degree one, and in particular does not have any rational point. To produce such examples, we use the theorem of \textit{A. S. Merkurjev} and \textit{A. A. Suslin} [Math. USSR Izv. 21, 307--340 (1983; Zbl 0525.18008)], the Riemann-Roch theorem over a surface and (for \(d=3)\) Rost's degree formula.

editorial_contributions.text: The main object of the paper under review is a smooth projective cubic surface \(X\) defined over a function field \(K=k(\Gamma )\) where \(k\) is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and \(\Gamma\) is an integral, smooth, projective curve over \(k\). The author proves that \(X\) satisfies weak approximation with respect to any finite set of places of good reduction. The methods are similar to those used in the arithmetic case by \textit{P.~Swinnerton-Dyer} [in: Rational points on algebraic varieties, Progr. Math. 199, Birkhäuser, 357--404 (2001; Zbl 1079.11035)]. Note that the result of the paper under review was generalized by \textit{B.~Hassett} and \textit{Y.~Tschinkel} [Invent. Math. 163, 171--190 (2006; Zbl 1095.14049)] to arbitrary rationally connected varieties using geometric techniques.

title.title: The Hadwiger-Nelson problem over certain fields

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(X\) be a smooth projective curve of genus \(g\geq 2\) over an algebraically closed field \(k\) of characteristic \(p>0\), and let \(F:X\to X_1\) be the Frobenius morphism. In this lecture the author first proves the following result. 


Theorem. If \(B_1\) is the sheaf of locally exact differentials on \(X_1\), then \(B_1\) admits a theta divisor (and in particular, \(B_1\) is semi-stable).


This result implies that the fundamental group \(\pi_1(X)\) has many \(k\)-representations of degree \(1\) which are ordinary. The author also gives examples of non-ordinary Galois covers of \(X\) with solvable Galois group of order prime to \(p\).

For the entire collection see [Zbl 0978.14002].

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The Arthur-Nimue-Merlin degrees are a generalization of the Turing degrees introduced by Kihara as a tangible description of the partially ordered set of Lawvere-Tierney topologies on the effective topos (equivalently, subtoposes of the effective topos). They are defined in terms of a three-player game that introduces both angelic and demonic non-determinism into oracle queries. We construct an order embedding of the Turing degrees with their order reversed into the Arthur-Nimue-Merlin degrees, whose image we call the ''co-Turing degrees''; we then study the order relationship of these co-Turing degrees with the (naturally embedded) Turing degrees within the Arthur-Nimue-Merlin degrees.

title.title: An order-reversing embedding of Turing degrees into Arthur-Nimue-Merlin degrees

editorial_contributions.text: The authors constructs algebraic geometric codes using anticanonically embedded del Pezzo surfaces over a finite field. The result (in the cases studied) greatly improves previous works, e.g. [\textit{J. A. Davis}, J. Pure Appl. Algebra, 215, No. 4, 496--510 (2012; Zbl 1205.14029); \textit{A. Couvreur} and \textit{I. Duursma}, Des. Codes Cryptography 66, No. 1--3, 291--303 (2013; Zbl 1263.94038)]. The authors focus on the rank \(1\) case for the Picard group over the base field. They give explicit constructions for del Pezzo surfaces of degree \(4\), \(5\) and \(6\), computing the parameters and the automorphism groups of the associated parameters. They obtain some codes with excellent parameters, the best ones accoding to codetables at the times of the submission, e.g., an \([13,7,5]\)-code over \(\mathbb {F}_4\).
